decision: PARTIAL -> W1 + W6: today's [3,6] is a Clemson (3) + RHS (6) union across two pages, which W6 forbids; one page's figure is authored. clemson_hgic carrot-beet-radish-parsnip states "When the parsnip plants are 1 to 2 inches tall, thin them to 3 inches apart for good root development." -> in_row [3,3]; "Rows are spaced 18 to 24 inches apart." -> row [18,24]. RHS 'leave one every 15cm (6in)' is the alternative point. Ten prose strings restating 3-6 (and the per-foot yield arithmetic) are re-authored to 3.

edits.new: Thin the seedlings to a final 3 inches apart once they are growing well, snipping the extras at the soil line. Keep weeds out, because slow parsnips do not compete well, and keep the soil evenly damp.
edits.reason: restates the moved in-row figure (Clemson: thin to 3 in)

edits.new: Thin to a final 3 inches once seedlings are well established, snipping at the soil line. Keep the bed weed-free, since slow parsnips compete poorly, and hold even moisture.
edits.reason: restates the moved in-row figure (Clemson: thin to 3 in)

edits.new: Once seedlings are well established, thin to a final 3 inches; snip at the soil line. Crowded parsnips stay small and forked.

edits.new: Thinning means pulling out some of the baby parsnips so the rest have room. Once the slow seedlings are a few inches tall and growing well, thin them to a final 3 inches apart. Snip the extras off at the soil line with scissors instead of pulling, so you do not disturb the ones you keep. Crowded parsnips stay small and twisted.
edits.reason: restates the moved in-row figure (Clemson: thin to 3 in)

edits.new: Thin parsnips to a final 3 inches apart once the slow seedlings are well established. (Clemson HGIC; Texas A&M AgriLife) Because germination is erratic and seed is sown fairly thickly to insure a stand, the row often comes up uneven and crowded; crowded roots stay small and misshapen. Snip the extras at the soil line rather than pulling, which disturbs neighbors. Larger-rooted varieties take the wider end of the spacing.
edits.reason: restates the moved in-row figure (Clemson: thin to 3 in)

edits.new: Each parsnip plant gives you one parsnip, the single long root it grows. So it helps to think about how much row you plant rather than per plant. Spaced 3 inches apart, a foot of row gives you roughly 4 big roots.
edits.reason: restates the moved in-row figure (Clemson: 3 in) and its per-foot arithmetic

edits.new: One root per plant. Parsnips are not a cut-and-come-again crop, so yield is best thought of by row length: at a 3 inch final spacing, expect roughly 4 large roots per foot of row, each often 8 to 12 inches long.
edits.reason: restates the moved in-row figure (Clemson: 3 in) and its per-foot arithmetic
